Man there really is no studio like this one. You can tell how passionate they are for that co-op experience. No microtransactions, a Friend's Pass that lets someone play with you for free, and a track record of great games. They really understands what makes couch co-op special. It's so refreshing to see a studio that has a clear vision that prioritizes making great games instead of trying to nickel and dime their customers. God bless Hazelight for keeping co-op alive.

[h2] Top-tier stuff [/h2]

Hazelight’s love for co-op is insane. Every game they drop feels like a passion project, and somehow, they just keep outdoing themselves. No greedy bs, no half baked ideas. Just pure, fun and well crafted co-op experiences. And they deliver x70 with every next game. Every penny spent feels earned.
[b] 10/10 [/b]

When it comes to value for money, this game shows the highest level of respect a studio can have for players. The $50 price tag in 2025 is honestly amazing for a game of this quality. Add in Friend Pass, which lets you play with your friends across different platforms, and the fact that there’s no Denuvo or annoying third party launchers that alone is a huge sign of respect toward gamers.

Story wise, I think it’s a bit weaker compared to It Takes Two and A Way Out, but that ending… absolutely mind blowing, creative, and emotional. I was honestly stunned.

Despite being made with Unreal Engine 5, the optimization is fantastic I didn’t run into a single issue.

My only real complaint is the lack of mini games. Unlike It Takes Two, which was full of fun little side activities, this one doesn’t have them but the amazing side missions make up for it pretty well.

With all the positives and the clear respect the devs have shown toward players, there’s no way I could give it anything less than a perfect score.

Thank you, Hazelight Studios.

[h1]Hazelight Delivers Again[/h1]

Hazelight is number 1 at co-op gameplay, and Split Fiction proves it. The game expands It Takes Two mechanics to present a fresh and enjoyable interactive cooperative experience. Just like It Takes Two, every section of the game introduces something new, keeping things fresh from start to finish. The level design is awesome. The gameplay is incredibly polished, and all the immensely various mechanics feel satisfying to play. Truly a peak game design showcase.

[h3]The Story – The Weakest Part of the Game[/h3]

The gameplay elements of the game outshine everything else because like It Takes Two, the narrative is the weakest part of the experience. Hazelight nailed this better in A Way Out and in Brothers, A Tale of Two Sons, which was a game that used no words to tell its story. The storytelling attempts from Split Fiction fall short because it tries too hard with emotional moments that don’t really land. It also is not goofy like It Takes Two. Split Fiction takes its story too seriously. The dialogue, the characters, they are just too predictable, too one-dimensional. After playing It Takes Two, and other Hazelight games, I was sure of what was gonna happen at the end 100%. And when that's the case, you can't really connect with the story since the writing is also kind of cliche and boring. The story stands as Split Fiction's main weakness though it does not reach unacceptable levels. To be honest, I just wanted to jump back into the gameplay.

[h3]Pacing Issues[/h3]

The pacing in It Takes Two was handled better than Split Fiction. In Split Fiction, some levels go on for way too long. The monkey and Groot level is an example of that. It just keeps going and going. The side stories in this game end at about 60-70% of the game but It Takes Two balanced its additional content across the entire game. Split Fiction doesn't have minigames (except the snow riding part) which is a negative, but there are side stories that were pretty insane in creativity. This issue is also to be seen in the later sections of the game, where you are presented with puzzles or puzzle-ish levels back-to-back, slowing down the game.

[h3]Graphics & Optimization – This is How UE5 Should Be Used[/h3]

Unlike many modern Unreal Engine 5 titles that are full of performance issues, Split Fiction runs amazingly. It doesn't have the disgusting render distance fog, no anti-color horrible filters, and remains a steady and high FPS at all times while looking amazing at all times. The art design is phenomenal. Every level is creatively mesmerizing and gorgeous without relying on Unreal Engine 5's lazy photorealism. And the game runs very well unlike the 20FPS UE5 slop we're seeing too often these days. Take notes, game devs!

[h3]A GOTY Contender, But Not the Winner[/h3]

Even though it's still too early to talk about Game of The Year in March, I think Split Fiction should and will be a nominee in The Game Awards this year. However, it's also It Takes Two 2.0, a refined, better version, but not something completely new like it was in It Takes Two. Which is why I think It Takes Two completely deserved the win in 2021. So that's why I don't think it should be Game of The Year since it's not going to be mine. My Game of The Year 2025 will probably be Death Stranding 2: On The Beach, or Grand Theft Auto VI if it releases this year, or Hollow Knight: Silksong? Who am I kidding? Silksong is not releasing this year :(

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]

I would love to play another one of these but I hope they will use their expertise to develop a fresh experience that revolutionizes another genre like they did with the co-op games. Hazelight is one of the few studios still doing great things in modern gaming and huge respect for EA for supporting them and giving them full creative freedom. The Friends Pass System is an amazing consumer-friendly move. Thank you, EA. I definitely recommend this at full price, since you can pay half with your friend.

Split Fiction is a game where you can feel the passion behind it in practically every minute you play. There is an almost ridiculous amount of creativity packed into it. Every level introduced some new idea, mechanic, visual style, and so much more—just when I thought I'd figured out what kind of game I was playing, it turned into another game entirely.

At various points, I was playing pinball, controlling shapeshifting robots, snowboarding for points, crossing between completely different worlds, solving wonderfully creative puzzles, and dealing with situations so absurd that we couldn't stop laughing. Then, somehow, the game managed to turn around and deliver moments that genuinely made us cry.

The side stories deserve particular praise because they were not just filler content, but rather little explosions of creativity in their own right that I doubt I'll experience anywhere else. The Halloween-themed one was my favourite, especially the flower-planting section. Some of the funniest moments in the game came from them! The main story itself develops in a way that pushes the game to further extremes; as the machine becomes increasingly unstable, the worlds themselves do so with it, and this progression gave the developers an excuse to get even more ambitious with what happens around you. Even the boss fights refused to settle into a formula. Every single one felt like a completely unique idea rather than a variation of the last, and then there was the finale...

I genuinely don't know how to describe it without ruining what makes it so special. It was completely and utterly mind-bending. The game took everything it had been doing and pushed it to its absolute limit.

Now, I've played a lot of games, but I don't think I've ever experienced anything quite like that sequence before. It was technically impressive, visually insane, incredibly imaginative, and one of those moments where I found myself wondering how somebody even came up with the idea in the first place.

But beyond all the mechanics and creativity, my favourite part of this game will always be the joy it engendered. There were evenings where I had to force myself to launch the game and start a session; I was miserable, tired, and struggling to motivate myself. But every single time we played, I felt energised, happy, distracted... and sure, maybe the happiness didn't always last very long after we stopped playing, but for those few hours... I was laughing, thinking, getting completely absorbed in whatever bizarre world the game had thrown us into next, and forgetting about everything else for a while.

I don't think every game needs to have some profound emotional impact on the person playing it, but for me, this one happened to arrive at a time when those treasured, fleeting little pockets of happiness genuinely mattered most, and that's probably the highest compliment I can give Split Fiction. It was not simply an incredibly creative co-op game. It was a game that constantly surprised me, made me laugh until I couldn't breathe, occasionally made me cry, and at times, even gave me something to look forward to.

You can feel the love that went into making this, and I hope you can feel the love I have for this game by reading this.

I think that in terms of Hazelight's library, Split Fiction is probably my least favorite of them to date. But for a studio like this, that's like naming your least favorite item on the menu of a five-star restaurant; either way, you're still getting good food. This is still some of the best co-op gaming on the market, and Josef Fares and his team still haven't lost their magic touch. 

Like their previous works, when Split Fiction is going great it repeatedly does things you've probably never seen in a game before, and when it's at its best it pulls stunts you might not have even thought were possible in a multiplayer context. There are some incredible stages and setpieces throughout the game, and those moments alone are worth the price of a ticket for two (which only requires one copy of the game, thanks to the usual friend pass system). The two protagonists' stories tend to start out pretty threadbare, but they do eventually build up to the obligatory heart-tugging drama that dares you to cry in front of a friend, and while the villain main is as cartoonish as it gets he's at least simple in an extremely funny way if you don't try to take it too seriously. 

When it isn't going great, though, the core problem is its inconsistency, especially early on. Where Brothers, A Way Out, and It Takes Two rarely had dull moments, Split Fiction occasionally gets bogged down in ideas that just aren't working very well. A lot of the early cyberpunk-inspired stages from Mio's side of things tend to just be an hour or so of fairly straightforward action platforming with few diversions, or a lengthy section where the only gimmick is that both players have laser guns that are mostly used for opening doors, and frankly the visual style for a lot of them hovers between "fake video game on a tv show" and "car insurance commercial". They're never bad enough to make you want to quit, but they sometimes feel too scripted and simple to feel genuinely exciting, and I think that's a shame in its own right. To me a large part of what made Hazelight's previous games so special was how seamlessly and frequently they moved between narrative gameplay, puzzles, action, and interactive diversions, and used a mix of their goofy gameplay gimmicks and competitive minigames to foster a very loose sense of cooperation that left the door wide open for all kinds of player-driven shenanigans. Split Fiction doesn't really have that; there are little crumbs of it every now and then, and the game does have brief side stories every now and then that give you a break from whichever half of the two flavors of stage you're currently in, but most of the parts that have that exceptional Hazelight spark are backloaded into the second half of the game. The silver lining is that they are more than worth the wait.

The other thing that surprised me is how much the story takes backseat most of the game, considering its concept. The premise of the game is that each stage is based on one of the protagonists' ideas for a novel, but the stages themselves rarely feel like something that would actually stem from that. I'm not saying I need the game to be Alan Wake, but in a lot of segments you're lucky if you have a story concept at all, and when you do it's rarely more than "we need to stop this bad guy", which is usually accomplished by just platforming your way forward and then killing them. For the first half of the game my partner and I genuinely couldn't tell if we were supposed to believe that either of the protagonists were even good at writing or if the point was supposed to be that there's a reason neither of them had been able to secure a publishing deal from anyone that wasn't trying to harvest their ideas into ChatGPT, and frankly even if the villain's plan had worked I think most of these story ideas would have just poisoned the dataset if anything. And while once again it's never a dealbreaker, I think that part of why the low points of the games end up being low points is because of this. It's understandable that in a co-op game you want the story to be light enough to not slow the gameplay down, but a lot of the standout moments in all three of their previous games were standout moments because of the way the story context amplified the meaning of what you were doing. A lot of the early stages have fancy setpieces like climbing a skyscraper or jumping along flying cars in a floating highway that end up feeling a little mundane because there's just no context to ground them in or give you a reason to care about anything more than Mio and Zoe moving forward and leaving, because the game's plot effectively starts at the halfway point.

None of this is to say that you shouldn't buy the game, because you absolutely should! It's fantastic. The only reason I'm nitpicking is because both my partner and I agreed that the amount of perfect score reviews this game has received set our expectations a bit higher than we maybe should have, and while it didn't sour our experience I think it's worth avoiding any sort of disappointment to focus on the things this game does really great instead. In my eyes, this is less a 10/10 masterpiece and more a very solid 8/10 game with individual bursts of 10/10 moments and rare 7/10 dips. If you've played their previous works and love them then maybe slightly adjust your expectations, but if this is your first Hazelight game, you might not even believe that it can get even better than this.

The gameplay is stress-free, with intuitive controls right from the start. I was hooked from the beginning as the game kept throwing unexpected, absurd, and funny moments my way, keeping the energy high and the surprises coming.

Visually, the game is artistic and stunning, especially on Zoe’s colorful side of the story. The narrative takes you on a journey that resonates with anyone who’s ever struggled with personal growth, grief or guilt all while maintaining the game’s playful spirit.

Equally impressive is the sound design, which excels despite the split-screen format. Distinct audio cues let you sense your partner’s actions without even looking at their side of the screen, making coordination feel effortless and enhancing the co-op experience.

One of the coolest features is the free friend’s pass, which works for cross-play PC/PlayStation via EA friend invite. Just keep in mind that the player using the friend’s pass won’t earn trophies, although I’m not sure about achievements on other platforms.

The overall experience bursts with childlike imagination, celebrating everything we love about video games. It’s a joyful tribute wrapped up in a fresh, creative package that keeps surprising you at every turn.

If I could give Split Fiction a 6/5, I would do it without hesitation and then ask if I could do it again. This game is absurdly good. One of the best two-player co-op games I have ever played, and honestly one of the best games I have played, period.

It feels like the devs looked at every other co-op game and said, “That’s cute, now watch this.” The amount of creativity packed into this thing is ridiculous. It is like 100 games stitched together by people who were clearly possessed by talent and caffeine. One minute you are in a sci-fi action sequence flying through chaos, the next you are deep in fantasy nonsense, and then suddenly you are a flying pig being launched by rainbow farts. And somehow, instead of feeling stupid, it feels incredible. That should not work. It absolutely does.

The craziest part is that the game never runs out of ideas. Every time I thought, “Okay, surely this is the gimmick for the next few hours,” it would turn around, slap me across the face with another mechanic, and make that one fun too. It just keeps going. It never feels lazy, never feels bloated, and never feels like it is wasting your time. In an industry full of games that overstay their welcome, Split Fiction had me begging for more.

After finishing it, I went back and tried the studio’s other games. A Way Out was amazing, It Takes Two was pretty good, but Split Fiction is the one that made me sit back and go, “Oh, these people are different.” This one is special.

If these devs really are making a three-player game next, then my group may need to notify work, family, society, and possibly emergency services that we will be unavailable.

Co op puzzle platformers are by no means my favorite kind of game. That said, I did enjoy Hazelight's previous game It Takes Two and loved A Way Out so seeing Josef Fares made a new game already gave me a lot to hope for. The setting and characters however didn't fill me with confidence when I first heard about the game as I didn't really know what to expect going in. 

I was however foolish to ever doubt Fares and his vision. So I can confidently say this game exceeded my expectations and then some. 

Split Fiction is much like It Takes Two. Except noticeably harder. And crazier. And dare I say much more fun overall if you can believe it. The amount of ideas and gimmicks and minigames put here is nothing short of amazing. Across various Sci Fi and Fantasy worlds the game manages to put you through various scenarios and stories allowing for a rich variety of gameplay quirks and always keeps you guessing what fun ability you and your co op buddy will get to use next. And the variety of gameplay elements and minigames is absolutely insane. You'll never see it coming. That's half the fun of this adventure though, the thrill of finding out what else can these people come up with and put it in videogame form, to say the people who made the levels and designed the gameplay did an amazing job would be an understatement. 

As far as puzzles go most of them are thankfully pretty straightforward. Though there have been a few times where me and my co op buddy were a bit stumped but that was fairly rare. 

In terms of the overall story, It was a fairly interesting one but nothing memorable. it does have some emotional moments which I found surprising but nothing that really moved me drastically. I want to quickly mention the last portion of the game, without going into detail. Absolutely bonkers. Just insane. [h1]Sights & Sounds[/h1]
[h3]Top-notch[/h3]
[list]
[*] You have to hand it to Hazelight; they know how to create visually interesting and often beautiful worlds to platform around in
[*] [i]It Takes Two[/i], despite taking place in a mundane suburban setting, looked lively and magical from its ankle-high [i]Honey, I Shrunk the Kids[/i] perspective. [i]Split Fiction[/i] further loosens the chains binding the design to reality by setting the whole game in a virtual environment
[*] Throughout the game, you'll alternate between cyberpunk dystopian sci-fi and magical high fantasy worlds springing from the minds of the two protagonists. Given the freedom provided by those two genres, environments and set pieces stay interesting and imaginative for the whole experience
[*] The whole thing looks fantastic even without a world-beating setup. My hardware would have been considered top-of-the-line in 2019, but it's starting to show its age with newer titles. The game still looked fantastic, thankfully
[*] The soundtrack leans into the disparate genres as well. I'd hesitate to call it generic, but you kinda already know what the auditory backdrop is going to to be. Sci-fi level? Prepare for exciting and energetic synth beats. Fantasy level? Hope you like lutes and woodwinds. Appropriate all around, but not exactly memorable
[*] As with Hazelights past titles, the voice acting is top-notch. There's a lot of back-and-forth between the two player characters, so it would have been frustrating had either had been poorly acted
[/list]

[h1]Story & Vibes[/h1]
[h3]Ehhhh...[/h3]
[list]
[*] If there's any blemish on what is otherwise an excellent co-op experience, it has to be the story. It's tropey, it's bland, and it's painfully uninteresting
[*] The narrative setup sounds pretty good on paper. An evil corporation has begun hiring aspiring authors and plopping them in virtual reality pods that allow them to inhabit the worlds of their stories
[*] That's a cool jumping off point, but there's hardly any exposition or explanation beyond that. What does the villainous CEO want to do with them? Movies? Video games? No clue, no one ever reveals that
[*] Why hook up authors to machines at all? Why not just buy their stories? I don't see how a giant sci-fi machine is supposed to help any sort of production process. It feels like a big, dumb, unnecessary expense. Anyone who invested in that idea deserves to lose their money
[*] And it doesn't get any better when you get into each protagonist's subplots. Without getting into the thick of it (there's no reason to), it's just to women who are bad at dealing with grief. I get it, I've lost loved ones too. It's an awful experience and things are never the same afterwards. But it's all just conveyed so poorly that both my wife and I were rolling our eyes constantly
[*] I think what we found so annoying was that it felt like Mio and Zoe appear to believe that their losses are unique and not something that every human will have to endure multiple times in the course of their lives. Even my wife, who lost her father just a few years ago, was scoffing and muttering at the screen for most of Mio's backstory reveal
[*] As an aside, I'm not a callous person. I'll never insist someone "get over it". Grief is labor. It is a burden you bear until you die and pass the weight onto your loved ones. You will not get over it, but you will learn to carry it better. But [i]Split Fiction[/i] seems to think that sharing your grief with another grieving person is sufficient. I promise you that doesn't always work
[*] Some may also point out that the writing for [i]It Takes Two[/i] was also poor and the plot was similarly generic, but at least the co-operative gameplay played nicely with the theme of collaboration. Here, the message is just a swing and miss
[*] Despite the theme of dealing with grief, most of the gameplay is exciting and fun. It feels a bit discordant
[/list]

[h1]Playability & Replayability[/h1]
[h3]Now for the good part[/h3]
[list]
[*] If you've played [i]It Takes Two[/i], you have a pretty good frame of reference for what's in store. Just imagine the same slick co-op platforming, but with a much greater focus on platforming than puzzling
[*] Oh, there's still plenty of puzzles, but prepare to have your reflexes, timing, rhythm, aiming, driving, and flying skills all tested to varying degrees depending on which protagonist you picked
[*] The reason that it matters is that there appears to be a greater focus on asymmetrical gameplay than in Hazelight's previous offering. While this can lead to some envy when your partner's power looks way more fun than what you got stuck with, it also leads to some memorable moments
[*] One such highlight was when I was dodging missiles in a building-traversing, gravity defying, [i]Distance[/i]-like chase sequence as Mio, my wife was fiddling on a smartphone with a malware resembling minigame in an effort to defuse a bomb as Zoe. We had a good laugh about that one
[*] Due to that dynamic, you'll probably find yourself screenwatching from time to time. Not only does it make it a little easier to coordinate some segments, it also allows you to catch a glimpse of what you're missing out on
[*] If you can get away with ignoring the bulk of the story, I'd call this an easily replayable game. Platforming through each colorful environment in this 12-16 hour title was irresistibly fun and addictive. My wife and I beat it over the course of a week or so and looked forward to playing for a bit each night
[/list]

[h1]Overall Impressions & Performance[/h1]
[h3]Still worth it[/h3]
[list]
[*] I tend to have strong opinions about writing in games, so the cornball dialogue and ho-hum placed a ceiling on my enjoyment. However, if you don't care about what a game tries to say, you're in for a lot of fun
[*] Even with the glaring fault, I still had a good time with the game at the end of the day. Hey, good platforming is good platforming, and it's even better when you get to share it with someone you like
[*] In the first section, I alluded to how great the game looks even on somewhat outdated hardware. It mostly runs fine too, but there are a few really cool visual segments towards the conclusion that unfortunately caused my framerate to tank a bit. Nothing unplayable, but it was noticeable
[/list]

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
- [b]8.0[/b]/10. Judging this game purely on the basis of its platforming mechanics, it's a stellar experience. As a vehicle for a story, it's a bit of a mess. Find something else to do during the cutscenes and you're in for a treat

As with It Takes Two, I played this local co-op with my daughter. For the first third, we thought it was mediocre; for the middle third, we thought comparable to It Takes Two; for the last third, giant dumb grins on our faces and "NO WAY!" "My brain hurts!" throughout.

I narrative frame is worse (in my view much worse) than It Takes Two, in part because the characters don't feel plausible (a fantasy author who knows nothing about scifi and vice versa? genre writers who are utterly genre-unsavvy as to their own predicament?) and in part because the lack of a preexisting relationship makes the bickering feel forced and the stakes wrong.

From the outset it's clear the story is a parable about generative AI, but what's odd is that the premise that you're going through stories written by the two human authors undermines the theme because those stories are so formulaic and the visuals are lifted so explicitly from preexisting works (many of the fantasy scenes are deliberate callbacks to Jackson's LOTR movies, for instance). If the idea is that humans are capable of genuine creativity that should be preserved and protected, shouldn't the internal stories feel more like novel works of genuine soul, rather than the kind of stories that generative AI itself could spit out with the right prompt? And what to make of the frame itself -- the real world outside the stories -- being perhaps even more cliche, with its power-mad tech CEO and the ominous board of directors lifted straight from The Avengers?

These flaws hold the game short of its potential, but ultimately it all clicks in the last third, where the difficulty finally gets where it should be, the levels combine all the gimmicks you've slowly been taught, and the story beats, even if predictable, land because they're timeless rather than timeworn, and supported by excellent art, music, and voice acting.

Easy to recommend this game; in sum it was a genuine joy and local co-op is always a blast. I hope the next foray from the dev goes closer to the Psychonauts-type framing of It Takes Two and the last third of Split Fiction, but despite my quibbles and qualms, if you're reading this review you should be playing the game instead.

Masterpiece and an easy 10 out of 10.

A Cooperative Masterpiece

 An exceptional cooperative experience that truly stands out in today's gaming landscape. This isn't just a game; it's a journey through meticulously crafted environments, brimming with diverse gameplay mechanics that constantly keep you and your fellow adventurers on your toes.

From the moment you dive in, the Lush, vibrant landscapes give way to grim, industrial complexes, and ancient, mystical ruins – each area rendered with incredible detail and a striking art style that truly brings the world to life. 

One moment you might be engaged in intense, fast-paced combat, chaining together abilities and coordinating attacks with your teammates. The next, you're faced with intricate environmental puzzles that demand creative problem-solving and seamless cooperation. There are stealth sections that require careful planning and synchronized movements, thrilling chase sequences,  This constant shift in mechanics prevents any feeling of monotony and ensures that every new area or mission presents a fresh, engaging challenge.


This isn't a game where cooperative play feels tacked on; it's intricately woven into every facet of the design. Many puzzles are explicitly designed for two or more players, requiring distinct roles and coordinated actions to overcome. 

Combat encounters often necessitate specific class abilities to be combined effectively, fostering genuine teamwork rather than simply having multiple players attacking the same target. The communication tools are intuitive, allowing for quick call-outs and strategic planning on the fly. 

Playing with friends feels incredibly rewarding, as you celebrate victories earned through true collaboration and laugh off the inevitable, chaotic blunders. The game even includes clever mechanics to help players who might fall behind, ensuring everyone can contribute and enjoy the experience.


Split Fiction is a testament to what cooperative gaming can achieve when executed with vision and precision. It's a gorgeous, mechanically rich adventure that constantly reinvents itself, all while keeping teamwork at its core. If you're looking for a game that will challenge your skills, ignite your strategic thinking, and forge unforgettable memories with friends, Split Fiction is an absolute must-play.

This game has gotten so much blind love from band wagoners, I figured I'd give a more level headed review. 

It takes two had so much variety and changes in gameplay that it felt like a defining feature of these types of games: that it's a game of games, if you played it takes two, you know what I mean. Split fiction is not that at all, it only changes about 2-3 times. The most notable one is the level "note book". I found this to be a huge let down, I LOVED that aspect of It Takes Two and FULLY expected Split Fiction to be the same.

Instead, Split Fiction is a story of stories, taking heavy inspiration from Halo, the movie gravity, tron, blade runner, and some other fantasy works. I find the premise of the game to be very awesome and full of potential, but the game falls far short in two areas: story telling INSIDE the sub stories, and variety of gameplay. 

SF does visuals INCREDIBLY well, which is where I think a lot of the impressed fans emerge from. The art, the animations, the lighting. Split Fiction does it all incredibly well, but it just doesn't do much of anything with it story and gameplay wise. It just seems like a bunch of really awesome, interesting art that doesn't have any depth to it, it's all hollow.

So what's the problem with SF? Why am I saying this?

 I would say 75% of the gameplay, start to finish of your 10+ hours of gameplay, is just simple, basic jump quests and simple puzzles that are CONSTANTLY recycled. I found this to be beyond infuriating given the price tag on the game.

The game feels like so much wasted potential. INSTEAD of giving all of the substories their own space and allowing those stories to develop, they are just drowned out by the main plot and not touched AT ALL. 

A great example is the level "Collapsing Star". You find yourself on a space station operating a dyson sphere harvesting power from a collapsing star. ( I assume almost some of that)

The level is BEAUTIFUL, the art is perfect, they NAIL the setting. The story however? totally abandoned. They do absolutely nothing with it. All you know is the star is dying, you have to stop it, and guess what, jump quests start to finish. There are no characters, no events, no context. It's rushed, it's basic, and it's hollow. Why is the star dying? Who and where are the scientists? Who owns the space station? Where are we?  Every single level is like this. There are NO characters except the protagonists and a boss on each level, few plot events, little to no context outside our protagonists dialog. The only thing in focus THE ENTIRE game is the sub plot of Mio and Zoe's interpersonal struggles building through the main plot of their conflict against Rader/ the corporation, Which I do really like. 

In execution though, I'd say they fail because it is a story about writers and their stories being stolen, but you only ever experience the simplified worlds they imagine, PACKED with jump quests and puzzles, not their stories. 

One thing I loved about the game though is the casual nature of it. The levels are all incredibly easy, in a charming way, and do give you a couple events here and there that take a few more tries, and then your're back to flying through the story, which doesn't bother me because there is so much content, and even flying through the game, you're getting well over 12 hours of content. 

So to end this poorly organized ramble, here's the take away:

Split Fiction is a very beautiful, artistic work with a solid MAIN PLOT, interesting settings, very mediocre/ HIGHLY recycled game play, with very under developed sub stories. I don't regret playing it, but I think if I knew exactly what I was buying/ didnt have my girlfriend wanting to play it, I probably wouldn't have bought it. 

The next game they make, which I really hope they do make another one, needs to be a GAME OF GAMES and a STORY OF STORIES, with depth, gameplay variety, and keeping that beautiful art work and level design.

Split Fiction is a fantastic video game and will continue to shine a spotlight on why Hazelight studios is the leading studio in co-op gameplay. Lets talk about it...

The Pros - 

Game play - Split Fiction has some of the most fun and addictive co-op game play you will experience. If you are familiar with hazelight studios you will know what to expect here, especially if you played It Takes Two. The games play nearly identical just with different mechanics and physics applied to this game and its levels. The game play is extremely addicting, rewarding and not overly harsh at all. 

Graphics - The game has a fantastic art style and overall has some of the best looking environments I have seen. The crossover between Fantasy and Sci-Fi really drives home the elements of the enviornments you play in. There are some settings that really make you go "wow" or "holy Sh*t" when you are first introduced to them. Overall this is not a ugly game to look at. 

Puzzles - Some of the best parts of this game is the puzzle solving but I admit they are relatively easy. It definitely ramps up towards the end of the game but overall they are solid and fun for two players to figure out. 

Replay Value - This game has fantastic replay value, between the ability to play two characters and obviously utilizing the co-op nature to play with new people. You MUST play this with a friend, it will make the experience infinitely better. 

Now lets talk about the cons - 

Story - The story in split fiction is not a bad story...its just not a good story either. It really is a overall mid story that was felt like just a excuse to keep the game play going which is the real winner here. I didn't connect with this story as much as i connected with their previous title It Takes Two. I feel like the story is one of the weaker parts of this game, but the game play more than makes up for it. 

Game Length - For the price charged, I don't feel the length is too egregious, however I do wish the game was at least 5 more hours longer. That would round it out really nicely in my opinion. 

Overall I highly recommend Split Fiction in its current form. It runs very smooth, with little to no issues. little to no bugs and will keep you laughing and playing for hours without realizing the time.
